sec: Subclinical hypothyroidism, myxoedema coma and review

items.q: Match the following follow-up plan — 1) Stable primary hypothyroidism 2) After dose change 3) Persistent symptoms despite normal TSH 4) Suspected non-compliance … A) Repeat TSH every 6–12 months B) Recheck TSH/FT3/FT4 at ~3 months C) Reassess adherence and drug interactions D) Re-evaluate diagnosis and consider T3 add-on
items.exp: Stable patients are monitored every 6–12 months; after dose changes recheck at 3 months; symptoms despite normal TSH prompt diagnosis review and possible T3 add-on; persistent abnormal labs are commonly due to non-compliance or interactions. (Book p909)

items.q: On levothyroxine 100 µg a patient's TSH remains elevated at 9 mIU/L despite claims of adherence. Which step is most consistent with the page?
opts: Assess adherence and drug interactions before increasing the dose
items.exp: Persistent abnormal TFTs are most often due to non-compliance or interfering drugs; investigate before titrating. (Book p909)

items.q: Assess follow-up intervals: I Re-check at 3 months after a dose change. II Once TSH normal, taper can be attempted cautiously.
items.exp: After dose changes, TSH is rechecked at about 3 months; once TSH normal, slow taper may be attempted in selected patients (e.g. transient thyroiditis). (Book p909)

items.q: Which is the odd one out — a transient cause where levothyroxine can eventually be tapered?
items.exp: Post-thyroidectomy hypothyroidism is permanent; the others are typically transient and may allow cautious taper once TSH normal. (Book p909)

items.q: Relief of hypothyroid symptoms typically occurs ___ months after TSH normalises.
items.exp: Symptomatic relief usually takes 3–6 months after biochemical normalisation; lipid and other parameters take longer. (Book p909)

items.q: Match the following emergency therapy for myxoedema coma — 1) First-line hormone 2) Steroid 3) Supportive measure 4) Trigger work-up … A) IV levothyroxine (often with liothyronine) B) IV hydrocortisone C) Active warming, electrolytes, ventilation D) Infection, MI, cold exposure, sedatives
items.exp: Myxoedema coma is treated with IV levothyroxine plus hydrocortisone (until adrenal insufficiency is excluded), supportive measures (warming, ventilation) and search for triggers (infection, MI, cold, sedatives). (Book p909)

items.q: An obtunded hypothyroid patient is started on IV levothyroxine. Why is hydrocortisone added concurrently?
opts: To cover possible coexisting adrenal insufficiency
items.exp: Concurrent adrenal insufficiency is possible; giving thyroid hormone first can precipitate adrenal crisis. Hydrocortisone is given until adrenal status is clear. (Book p909)

items.q: Assess myxoedema coma: I Active external rewarming is the recommended initial step. II IV levothyroxine should be withheld until adrenal insufficiency is excluded.
items.exp: Active rewarming can precipitate arrhythmia; passive rewarming is preferred. Levothyroxine should not be withheld — both levothyroxine and hydrocortisone are started empirically. (Book p909)

items.q: Match the following common trigger of myxoedema coma — 1) Infection 2) Cold exposure 3) Sedatives 4) MI … A) Most common precipitant B) Winter decompensation C) CNS depressant D) Cardiovascular collapse
items.exp: Infection is the most common trigger; cold exposure causes winter decompensation; sedatives depress CNS; MI can precipitate cardiovascular collapse. (Book p909)

items.q: A hypothyroid patient with persistent symptoms despite normal TSH on levothyroxine 100 µg asks about adding T3. Which is the source's most consistent response?
opts: Combination T4/T3 is not standard; review adherence and interactions first
Increase T4 dose beyond weight-based target
items.exp: Combination therapy is not routinely recommended; first rule out adherence and drug interactions, then re-evaluate the diagnosis. (Book p909)

items.q: Persistent abnormal TFTs on adequate doses of levothyroxine are most often due to ___ or drug interactions.
items.exp: Non-compliance is the most common cause of persistently abnormal TFTs on replacement; drug interactions and malabsorption are close seconds. (Book p909)

items.q: Assess these caveats: I Desiccated thyroid is the source's preferred long-term replacement. II Liothyronine has a longer half-life than levothyroxine.
items.exp: Levothyroxine is the standard; liothyronine has a shorter half-life than levothyroxine. (Book p909)

items.q: Which is the odd one out among reversible causes of hypothyroidism that may allow taper?
items.exp: Hashimoto is permanent; the others are typically transient and may allow cautious taper. (Book p909)
